news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

The Giants’ ever-changing quarterback situation is testing offensive coordinator Matt Nagy’s math skills.

Get texts from Paul Schwartz with all the latest Giants news and insights, exclusive to Sports+ subscribers.

Nagy estimated that the Giants lost about 30 percent of their playbook — namely, the dual-threat quarterback section of zone reads and RPOs — when Jaxson Dart was injured in Week 2 and replaced by pocket passer Jameis Winston for four starts.

The latest variable in the equation is the introduction of J.J. McCarthy, who leapfrogged Winston to get the next start Sunday against the Texans.

“Maybe now 20 percent of that 30 that was gone is back,” Nagy said before Thursday’s practice. “For us, what does he do well? You’ve seen some of the packages he’s done, but that can become predictable. We don’t want to be predictable. Now that he’s the starter, it probably benefits us some that he’s just not always coming in to do predictable QB-driven runs.”

Making just his second appearance since he was acquired in a Sept. 28 trade from the Vikings, McCarthy produced a historic fourth quarter — 243 passing yards and three scoring drives — off the bench last Sunday in nearly bringing the Giants back from a 24-point deficit in a 34-27 loss to the Saints.

The performance backed up the coaching staff’s belief that McCarthy turned a corner last week and was ready for a bigger role.

“Just the confidence of him being able to, in practice, talk to us about the scheme, where his eyes are going in the pass game, where he’s snapping the ball with a motion or a shift,” Nagy said.

“If there was a shoestring with Jameis or he got hurt, he could go in and function. Whereas the first two weeks, I had a highlighted [play] call sheet that, if something happened and he was in, these were the plays. It was probably 50 percent. Last week, it was probably 90 percent. Now this week, it’s going to be 100 percent.”

Tight end Isaiah Likely said it is the responsibility of the other 10 offensive players to make McCarthy “as comfortable as can be [for] a quarterback in a new offense.”

McCarthy has at least two pass catchers who believe they are always open. So, he’ll throw his 50 mph fastballs — among the fastest quarterback velocity in the league — downfield (12.4 career yards per completion) against a notoriously ball-hawking secondary.

“Letting him know that as long as the ball’s in the air and in my vicinity, it’s a great pass either way,” Likely said. “It doesn’t matter if somebody’s on me or if I’m wide open. Just throw the ball, trust me, and I’m going to make the play for you.”

McCarthy is the eighth quarterback that Malik Nabers has caught a pass from in 25 career games. His strategy for adapting to quarterback change is simple.

“Get open; just get open,” Nabers said. “They’re going to find you, and they know who their guys are. And when you talk to them, just give motivation to them. Tell them, ‘I know you’re just coming in, you don’t know me, really … but just know on certain plays, just give me an opportunity. Even when I’m covered, just give me an opportunity.’ ”

Sign up for Inside the Giants by Paul Schwartz, a weekly Sports+ exclusive.

Please provide a valid email.

By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

Enjoy this Post Sports+ exclusive newsletter!

McCarthy aced the no-huddle part of the playbook against the Saints. But what about managing a four-quarter game?

“His operation is really, really good,” Nagy said. “It starts with listening to the play call in your headset, being able to say it and/or read it on the wristband, get to the line of scrimmage, and then be a quarterback: see the formation, motion shifts, see the play clock, make your ID checks or whatever you do with the center, and then make a play. What he’s doing is amazing. He wants as much as he can get to digest within our offense.”

The Giants could have not thrown McCarthy into a hostile road environment as 9.5-point underdogs and given him two weeks to prepare to make his first start after the bye. Why wait?

“We would not have had the discussion if we didn’t think he could do it,” Nagy said. “We fully feel as a staff [quarterbacks] coach [Brian] Callahan has done an amazing job working with him and getting him ready. We feel confident about it.”

Making just his second appearance since he was acquired in a Sept. 28 trade from the Vikings, McCarthy produced a historic fourth quarter — 243 passing yards and three scoring drives — off the bench last Sunday in nearly bringing the Giants back from a 24-point deficit in a 34-27 loss to the Saints.

The performance backed up the coaching staff’s belief that McCarthy turned a corner last week and was ready for a bigger role.

“Just the confidence of him being able to, in practice, talk to us about the scheme, where his eyes are going in the pass game, where he’s snapping the ball with a motion or a shift,” Nagy said.

“If there was a shoestring with Jameis or he got hurt, he could go in and function. Whereas the first two weeks, I had a highlighted [play] call sheet that, if something happened and he was in, these were the plays. It was probably 50 percent. Last week, it was probably 90 percent. Now this week, it’s going to be 100 percent.”

Tight end Isaiah Likely said it is the responsibility of the other 10 offensive players to make McCarthy “as comfortable as can be [for] a quarterback in a new offense.”

McCarthy has at least two pass catchers who believe they are always open. So, he’ll throw his 50 mph fastballs — among the fastest quarterback velocity in the league — downfield (12.4 career yards per completion) against a notoriously ball-hawking secondary.

“Letting him know that as long as the ball’s in the air and in my vicinity, it’s a great pass either way,” Likely said. “It doesn’t matter if somebody’s on me or if I’m wide open. Just throw the ball, trust me, and I’m going to make the play for you.”

McCarthy is the eighth quarterback that Malik Nabers has caught a pass from in 25 career games. His strategy for adapting to quarterback change is simple.

“Get open; just get open,” Nabers said. “They’re going to find you, and they know who their guys are. And when you talk to them, just give motivation to them. Tell them, ‘I know you’re just coming in, you don’t know me, really … but just know on certain plays, just give me an opportunity. Even when I’m covered, just give me an opportunity.’ ”

McCarthy aced the no-huddle part of the playbook against the Saints. But what about managing a four-quarter game?

“His operation is really, really good,” Nagy said. “It starts with listening to the play call in your headset, being able to say it and/or read it on the wristband, get to the line of scrimmage, and then be a quarterback: see the formation, motion shifts, see the play clock, make your ID checks or whatever you do with the center, and then make a play. What he’s doing is amazing. He wants as much as he can get to digest within our offense.”

The Giants could have not thrown McCarthy into a hostile road environment as 9.5-point underdogs and given him two weeks to prepare to make his first start after the bye. Why wait?

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Josh Hart spent five years going at it with Mitchell Robinson in practice. Now, they’re about to do it in a real game, on opposing teams.

Friday night against the Celtics in Boston will be the first time the Knicks face Robinson since he left in free agency.

He signed a three-year, $47.4 million deal — a number the Knicks couldn’t come close to matching under the edict from owner James Dolan to stay under the second apron — to be a new addition to Boston’s starting lineup.

“It’s gonna be the same thing,” Hart said after Knicks practice Thursday. “We’re still gonna be battling for rebounds.”

Hart, who knows the Celtics like to have their center guard the opposing team’s worst shooter — a treatment he’s become accustomed to — is particularly excited for one facet of the matchup.

“They crossmatch a lot, so I’m sure he’ll be guarding me,” Hart said. “When I make a couple, I’m gonna let him know.”

Jokes aside, it will be a special moment for the Knicks to see Robinson, who had been the longest-tenured Knick on their championship roster, having spent the first eight years of his career with the organization.

“It’s bittersweet,” Karl-Anthony Towns said Thursday, “because you love Mitch. We’ve done so much historical things together here. To not see him in a Knicks jersey anymore, obviously, for all of us, we’re a family unit. You guys are around us every day; you know how much we care about each other, each other’s families, and to not be able to have him with us on this journey after that amazing journey we went through is obviously bittersweet. But it’s gonna be amazing to be able to see our brother, to hug him, be able to show him some love and to obviously compete playing basketball, like we love to do.”

Robinson’s impact extended off the court for the Knicks. He was one of the biggest personalities in the locker room.

“It’s definitely different [without him],” Hart said. “Obviously, that’s someone who’s had a big presence here, big presence in the locker room. It’s different. No one else listens to country [music] but me, so that’s tough in the weight room. The lack of his presence is obviously felt a little bit. That’s why it’s a new team.”

For his own part, Robinson did not exactly wax poetic about facing the Knicks.

“It doesn’t matter that I’m playing my former team,” Robinson said. “It’s more so trying to bounce back from what happened two nights ago. At the end of the day, it’s basketball; it’s a business. You gotta play the team just like you play any other team.”

Robinson struggled in the Celtics’ season-opening loss to the Pistons on Tuesday, recording four points and three rebounds in 18 minutes.

“I played like ass,” Robinson said. “It’s kind of just straightforward.”

He was too fed up with his performance to watch the Knicks’ championship ceremony.

“I was still stuck in my head from last game,” Robinson said. “I’m proud of those guys, obviously; I was a part of it. I just didn’t really want to watch it.”

Robinson is expected to receive his ring, accompanied by a tribute video, when he returns to MSG for the Knicks-Celtics game on March 14.

The Knicks certainly know better than anyone else what to expect from Robinson, with his offensive rebounding prowess and ability to guard all positions on the court. The same goes, of course, for his brutal free-throw shooting, which became a recurring storyline in recent years. Opposing teams, particularly in the playoffs, often utilized Hack-a-Mitch to exploit his weakness.

Will the Knicks now flip the script and use it on him?

“Maybe,” head coach Mike Brown said. “I think that’s more, just me personally, I’ve always leaned more to do that come playoff time or later in the [regular] season where you’re really trying to game plan and get certain games. Right now, I want to see if we can defend these guys with what we do staple-wise, with what our foundation is.”

Sign up for Inside the Knicks by Stefan Bondy, a weekly exclusive on Sports+.

Please provide a valid email.

By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

Enjoy this Post Sports+ exclusive newsletter!

It will be weird for Knicks fans to root against Robinson after all the ups and, for most of the beginning of his career, downs he went through with the team.

“At the end of the day,” Brown said, “we want to kick his ass like he probably wants to kick ours.”

news.originalContent:
Brandi Glanville is preparing to have her “face taken off” this week amid her ongoing battle with facial disfigurement.

The “Real Housewives of Beverly Hills” alum revealed the “great news” on Thursday’s episode of her “Brandi Glanville Unfiltered” podcast, saying she will undergo the drastic procedure Friday.

“Dr. Carlo Henrado is taking my face off on Friday and going to do an exploratory surgery to kind of do a power wash under my skin,” Glanville, 53, told her co-host, James Maas.

She said the doctor had identified two distinct spots beneath her skin that he believes could be either “fungal balls or something alive.”

“I think it’s alive, personally, because it moves when it wants,” she added.

Glanville went on to explain that Henrado came “highly recommended” and agreed to perform the procedure for whatever amount insurance would cover, plus an additional $5,000.

“But I’m OK with that. He’s like, ‘If I can cut the head off the beast, the snake, then the other stuff we’ll be able to get,” she continued.

The former model admitted that she’s “super excited” but also “scared to death,” as she’s “never had facial surgery.”

She noted that a woman she knows recently underwent a facelift, but said her own procedure is different and “more intensive,” according to her doctor.

Sign up for Virtual Reali-Tea with Danny and Evan, our must-read newsletter!

Please provide a valid email.

By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

Want more celebrity and pop culture news?

“He’s, like, literally going in there with a power washer, basically, and knives and all this s–t. And then he’s spinning my blood and doing this platelet thing on the inside of my face,” Glanville explained before joking, “We might not want my blood at this point.”

Last month, Glanville revealed she had been diagnosed with multiple conditions after years of unexplained health issues, including “highly resistant ESBL Klebsiella and Enterobacter with biofilm, Coccidioidomycosis (Valley fever), Demodex dermatitis and mononucleosis.”

She also previously disclosed that she had a fungal ball in her face that she was preparing to have surgically removed.

The reality TV star shared footage of an ultrasound on Instagram in early September, claiming her doctors “saw something alive” and “moving” beneath the skin of her face.

“If I don’t find a doctor to cut this out of my face, I’m just going to do it myself,” she said in the Reel at the time.

Glanville first blamed Bravo for her facial disfigurement in 2024, later claiming doctors suspected a “parasite that jumps around [her] face,” while others attributed her symptoms to “stress-induced edema.”

In February, she instead blamed her 20-year-old breast implants — which she said had “ruptured” and “leak[ed] silicone into her lymph nodes” — for her ongoing health struggles.

Glanville later revealed she had been diagnosed with a benign facial tumor “in one of [her] lymph nodes in [her] face.”

news.originalContent:

TORONTO — The correlation between Alexis Lafrenière’s expanded role and the strongest start of his NHL career is evident.

It wasn’t until his seventh season that the 2020 No. 1 overall pick was deployed on the top line, skated on the first power play unit and logged nearly 20 minutes of ice time a night, almost every night, from Day 1 of a new campaign.

Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Mollie Walker about the inside buzz on the Rangers.

There’s no use in rehashing all the reasons why it unfolded this way. The logjam of top-six forwards ahead of him when he was drafted is well documented and the inconsistencies in his game that made it difficult to entrust him with such assignments are known.

Through his first three and a half weeks with such responsibilities, however, Lafrenière has thrived.

“I think he’s opened up — or developed — other aspects of his offensive game,” head coach Mike Sullivan said Thursday before the Rangers took on the Maple Leafs at Scotiabank Arena. “In particular, his grind game down low in the offensive zone. He’s always been a guy that’s been dangerous off the rush. He’s a talent. He’s a talented player. Rush offense tends to be talent-driven. But one of the things that I try to challenge him with, when I first became the coach here, was the better teams in the league a lot of times they get numbers back, they take the rush away. So then what? How do you produce offense, right? I try to challenge him on his down-low game.

“He’s a lean guy, but he’s hockey strong. He’s so capable of creating offense from below the goal line, hanging on to pucks, rolling off of checks, and making next plays, getting inside at the net and creating off of a loose puck at the net front. He’s got a great stick. He sees it extremely well and he’s strong. We’ve tried to challenge him as a coaching staff in developing that aspect of his game. I think when you look at the second half of the season last year and continuing through this year, that’s the biggest area of his game that I think we’ve seen the biggest growth.”

Not only was Lafrenière tied for seventh in the NHL with seven goals entering Thursday’s game, but the 25-year-old led the Rangers in goals and points (13). He had posted at least one point in seven of his prior eight games, including a six-game point streak that tied the longest of his career.

His four multipoint games this season — including an empty-net abetted hat trick against the Islanders earlier this month — were the most of the Blueshirts and tied for the 11th most in the league.

Sign up for Inside the Yankees by Greg Joyce, exclusively on Sports+.

Please provide a valid email.

By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

Enjoy this Post Sports+ exclusive newsletter!

Sullivan said he thinks Lafrenière has “made a concerted effort” in the game down low since the start of the season.

Now, Lafrenière is averaging just under a minute and a half more ice time than last season. His increased involvement in the Rangers’ game has led to an increased output of production and on-ice impact.

“I don’t think there’s any question, I think [his expanded role] helps,” Sullivan said. “One of the things that I said to him when I became the coach was … we had a long conversation before we even stepped on the ice. We all wanted to try to help him build his game and get his game to another level, and he agreed. Part of my job, I think as the coach, is I got to provide a pathway for that player to do so. And so that’s what I’ve tried to do.

“He’s getting significant power play time, he’s playing in the top six. And to his credit, he’s taken advantage of it. He’s done a terrific job.”

news.originalContent:
Demonstrators gathered on the sixth anniversary of a near-total abortion ban imposed by Poland’s highest court.

Thousands of people have protested in more than 20 towns and cities across Poland, calling for access to free and legal abortion services.

Demonstrators gathered on the sixth anniversary of a near-total abortion ban imposed by Poland’s highest court.

Currently, abortion is only legal in Poland when a pregnancy results from a criminal act like rape or incest, or when it threatens the life or health of the mother.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s government promised to liberalise abortion laws ahead of its 2023 election victory, but divisions within the coalition have slowed progress.

The demonstrations come days after parliament passed two bills that would ease abortion restrictions in the mostly Catholic country, but are likely to be vetoed by Poland’s conservative President Karol Nawrocki.

Passing the draft laws now, a year before the next parliamentary election, is a case of “token gestures” rather than a genuine effort to reform abortion law, said Zofia Marcinek of the Abortion Dream Team, a reproductive rights activist group in Warsaw.

She said the liberal government knew the draft laws stand no chance of withstanding Nawrocki’s veto, and has merely tried to create the impression of taking action because it needs women’s support to win elections next year.

In the capital, Warsaw, about 1,000 protesters demonstrated in front of parliament despite rain.

“Over the last six years, nothing has really changed,” said 36-year-old Emilia Niemiec, who manages the AboTak abortion centre, which provides women with access to resources, including pills, and a space to be able to seek support or carry out a pharmacological abortion.

Restrictive abortion laws have been in place in Poland since 1993, with Polish women leading calls for the legalisation of abortion ever since. In 2016, nationwide demonstrations took place, with women donning black as a sign of protest.

But rather than being relaxed, Poland’s abortion laws were tightened further, banning abortions of foetuses with congenital defects in 2020 under the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government.

Despite the laws, abortions remain common in Poland, with the overwhelming majority carried out by women at home using pills obtained from outside the country. Women who undergo abortions, including by taking pills, do not face criminal responsibility under Polish law. But people helping them, including doctors and family, can potentially be prosecuted.

Polish hospitals performed 573 abortions in the first half of 2026, compared with 452 in the whole of 2022 before Tusk came to power, according to data from the National Health Fund. But activists say tens of thousands of abortions happen yearly outside of hospitals.

“The government’s promises act as a type of disinformation,” Marcinek said. “Women getting pregnant hear the prime minister say that everything is OK, that there is access to abortion, and then they end up in the hospital and see that is not the case. So they come to us when it’s very late and very complicated and expensive to help them.”

Protests in several cities ​coincide with a deepening economic, social and political crisis in Tunisia.

Tunisian police have clashed with protesters in rare unrest in the capital city of Tunis, as well as ⁠⁠in the southern town of Jebiniana, over recent deaths linked to the police.

Police forces fired tear gas on Thursday to disperse protesters in ⁠⁠Ettadhamen, a suburb ⁠⁠of the capital, following the death of a man detained on suspicion of drug dealing.

The man’s family said he died as a result of abuse by police officers after his arrest, ‌‌calling for the circumstances of his death to be clarified and those responsible to be held accountable.

Local media, however, reported that he died after swallowing drugs.

Protesters blocked roads, burned tyres and threw stones at police. Security forces responded by firing tear gas while seeking ⁠⁠to secure a National Guard station in ⁠⁠the area, the Reuters news agency reported.

In Jebiniana, in Sfax governorate, police clashed with protesters following the death of a man whose relatives said he had died while being chased by security forces.

Tunisian media reported that protesters set a vehicle ablaze and burned tyres, while police used tear gas against the protesters.

Students in the coastal city of Sfax protested another civilian death, this time blaming ambulance services for the death of a female student who suffered a cardiac problem.

Her colleagues said ambulance personnel took too long to arrive, citing a lack of medical facilities, and ‌‌called for a strike at Sfax University’s faculties on Friday.

The flare-ups on Thursday coincide with a deepening economic, social and political crisis in Tunisia, heightening ⁠⁠fears of a wider wave of violent protests as anger grows over deteriorating living conditions and poor public services.

Thousands of Tunisians joined the largest protest against President Kais Saied in years in the ‌‌capital ‌‌on Saturday, accusing him of undermining democracy and mishandling the economy in a growing challenge to his rule.

A Tunisian military court on Wednesday sentenced opposition ⁠⁠politician Olfa ⁠⁠Hamdi to four years in prison on charges of plotting against state security and inciting the ⁠⁠military to disobey orders, the latest move against opponents of ⁠⁠Saied.

news.originalContent:
The world authority on threatened wildlife classified 96 percent of all coral reef systems as "critically endangered".

Almost all of the world’s shallow-water coral reefs face an extremely high risk of collapse in the next 50 years, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) has warned in a new global assessment.

In a report released on Thursday, the world authority on threatened wildlife classified 96 percent of the planet’s coral reef systems as “critically endangered”, its highest risk category, with total extinction possible by 2075.

“The future threat of climate change is looming and severe, and that poses a very high risk to the survival of these ecosystems,” said Mishal Gudka, scientific lead of the IUCN Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment.

Corals are heat-sensitive and particularly vulnerable to human-driven climate change, which is warming the world’s oceans and increasing the frequency and intensity of damaging bleaching events.

When a reef collapses, hard corals disappear and are replaced by algae, rubble and sponges. As a result, the reef no longer supports a diverse ecosystem that can include everything from tiny invertebrates to reef fish like grouper.

The emergence this year of a “super” El Nino, the natural warming phenomenon, also presents a risk to corals, Gudka said at a news conference at the UN’s COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia.

It’s the latest dose of bad news for coral reefs, which are critical sources for seafood and tourism and often serve as buffers against coastal erosion and storms.

Sometimes dubbed “rainforests of the sea”, they have some of the world’s richest biodiversity and support a quarter of marine species as well as coastal communities and businesses.

Most of the world’s famous reef systems – including the Great Barrier Reef in Australia, the Coral Triangle in the Western Pacific Ocean and Southeast Asia, the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System and the Red Sea coral reefs – are critically endangered, according to the assessment.

For its report, the IUCN used the “middle-of-the-road” scenario from the UN’s panel of climate experts that projects global temperatures rising 2.7C above pre-industrial levels by 2100.

Its analysis examined 127 tropical and subtropical coral systems covering 188,362 square kilometres.

A week ago, another IUCN study in the journal Nature found that nearly 44 percent of reef-building coral species face an elevated risk of extinction due to climate change. A year ago, a survey found that harmful bleaching of the world’s coral had grown to include 84 percent of the ocean’s reefs, the most intense of its kind in recorded history.

Despite its warning, the IUCN said coral reefs in most parts of the world “are not yet lost”.

“Coral reefs have shown a remarkable ability to bounce back from devastating bleaching events,” said Gudka. “Pockets of surviving, resilient coral reefs can still remain in the future, so we must do everything within our reach to set them up for success.”

news.originalContent:
Hundreds of Ethiopians have crossed into Kenya, fleeing ⁠⁠fighting in ⁠⁠the border town of Moyale, which was reportedly prompted by loyalists publicly raising the flag of a neighbouring majority-Somali state.

Kenyan police said on Thursday that hundreds of Ethiopians, mostly women and children, crossed into Kenya through several entry points in Moyale, including the Sessi, Kore, Biashara, Foundation and Miti areas.

The people who crossed the border were fleeing tensions between leaders of Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regional states, according to Kenyan police.

The police reported gunfire and chaotic scenes in Moyale.

Ethiopian media reported that the fighting in Moyale started as a dispute over raising the flag of the Somali Regional State, a regional state in eastern Ethiopia, on Sunday.

Tensions escalated into fighting between forces from the Oromia and Somali regions.

The Kenya Red Cross said it was setting up temporary shelter and distributing essential items including cereal and porridge flour.

“The response will initially reach 1,000 households,” the Kenya Red Cross said in a statement on Thursday.

It added that experts were conducting an assessment to work out how many people were ⁠affected and what their needs were.

The regional clash is hundreds of kilometres away from ‌‌a larger conflict in the northern Tigray region between government forces and a rebel alliance led by the Tigray People’s ‌‌Liberation ‌‌Front.

news.originalContent:
The prize comes less than two weeks after US President Donald Trump announced sanctions against the court.

The European Union has awarded the International Criminal Court (ICC) its top human rights award, two weeks after US President Donald Trump vowed to dismantle the court through new sanctions.

Thursday’s Sakharov Prize is the second international recognition for the war crimes tribunal this month, with former ICC Judge Navi Pillay awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her work to promote peace and international law.

“The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognises the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice,” said European Parliament President Roberta Metsola in announcing the award.

The ICC thanked the European Parliament for the honour “at a time when the Court and its officials face unprecedented challenges”.

“Against this backdrop, the Sakharov Prize carries particular significance, reaffirming the importance of independent judicial institutions and of those who work to uphold international law,” ICC President Tomoko Akane said.

The Hague-based ICC has long been a target of Trump, whose campaign against it has escalated since the court announced in 2024 arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant.

The Trump administration has promised to dismantle the court “brick by brick”, recently announcing sanctions aimed at crippling its day-to-day operations. The ICC tries individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.

“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us because our message is clear: the United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a video posted on social media when the sanctions were announced.

Washington has also sanctioned ICC judges and prosecutors, as well as a UN special rapporteur focusing on the occupied Palestinian territories and Palestinian rights groups that have provided evidence to the court.

The EU has already thrown its support behind the ICC in the face of the US sanctions, which are due to come into force in six months, and has said it is “ready to take any necessary measures” to make sure the court can continue functioning.

“The International Criminal Court must be free to pursue its mission, independently, and without pressure or intimidation,” EU chief Ursula von der Leyen posted online after the prize was announced.

Brussels is hoping to use the delay before the sanctions are applied to try to talk the US down, but according to EU officials is also eyeing implementing a “blocking statute” to shield the ICC from Washington.

Two diehard Knicks fans have gone viral for reportedly naming their newborn after the team’s unforgettable championship run.

Yvonne Gonzalez-Bradford and Vance Bradford welcomed their first son, “Knickson Fyve Bradford,” on Aug. 8 after New York’s historic NBA Finals victory over the San Antonio Spurs this summer, the couple told Today this week.

The idea for the name came after the Bradfords opened the windows of their Long Island City high-rise apartment and heard elated revelers chanting “Knicks in five!”–  after the team clinched their first title in 53 years, the outlet reported.

The next day, Bradford recalled his wife looking at him and asking, “What if we give our son a name for a champion? What about Knickson?”

Gonzalez-Bradford, who was 7 months pregnant at the time, later suggested Fyve as Knickson’s middle name.

“Five is also an indivisible number. So he’s our indivisible champion,” the mom said.  “You can hear him cooing in the background right now.”

Bradford’s late mother, Sydell Johnson, was the scorekeeper for the team during their last championship in 1973. She passed away unexpectedly last year, making Knickson’s arrival all the more significant for the family.

“I’m like, ‘Oh my gosh, Ma, you went up there and you sent us one,’” he said. “She sent down a Knicks championship!”

The little champion has since gone viral on Instagram, racking up hundreds of thousands of views and a repost from Spike Lee of pictures of him swaddled in Knicks gear with a plush basketball by his side.

“If he turns out to be a Celtics fan or a Sixers fan, again he’s still Knickson Bradford, who is in the boardroom,” the dad said.

“We wanted to have a very strong and firm name that would lead to a cool life. Knickson Fyve is definitely our motto. Knickson Fyve forever!”

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

The end of the work week has become become just another weeknight, with Americans now spending just 4% of their evenings with their friends, according to a depressing new study.

Late-night socializing after midnight — once a defining part of weekend social life — has all but vanished as well, dropping below 1% of their time, according to a recent study by Neal Caren from the Department of Sociology at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill.

Between the early 2000s and 2024, total expected weekly time with friends fell by more than half, according to the study, built using data from the American Time Use Survey.

In 2003, the first date of measured data, social life followed a predictable weekly “heartbeat,” Caren wrote.

Weekday evenings saw modest socializing, peaking at around 6 to 7% of time, which steadily built toward sharp weekend peaks of 9% on Friday and 12% on Saturday nights, the study found.

Late-night socializing past midnight was also common on weekends, according to the data.

But this isn’t just a COVID-19 story. Starting in the mid-2010s, Friday night social time saw a steep decline.

The share of Friday evening time spent with friends fell from 9% in 2003-2005 to 7% in 2017-2019, dropping to 4% during the post-pandemic years of 2022-24.

Friday night social interaction today barely exceeds a typical Thursday weeknight, the study found.

Saturday remains the most social night of the week, but its peak friend-time share dropped as well, from 12% in 2003-2005 to 7% in 2022-2024.

Saturday’s social peak today sits at around the same level Friday nights used to hold two decades ago, the study found.

Also stark is the disappearance of the late night, with socializing past midnight now all but gone for American adults.

Total expected weekly time with friends fell from roughly 350 minutes per week in 2003-2005 to about 170 minutes in 2022-2024, the study found.

This contraction occurred across the entire week and across all types of social activities, rather than shifting to different days or alternative activities.

These included socializing and social events, relaxing and watching TV with friends, arts and entertainment, sports and exercise, and other social activities.

The “homeward retreat,” as Caren described it, was most noticeable among younger, more-educated, and unmarried adults, with an outsized impact on single adults.

It comes as a separate chart found that almost every form of social activity in America has dropped over the last 30 years.

The percentage of American adults who entertained people at their home in the past year fell from 88% in 1995 to 67% in 2026, according to a study by Data for Progress.

The percentage of Americans who obtained a church or other place of worship in the past year fell from 74% to 54% in the same time period, and the percentage of those who gave or attended a dinner party fell from 70% to 57%.

In contrast, the percentage of those who played a home video game rose from 42% in 1995 to 64% in 2026, and those went to an exercise class rose from 18% to 32% in the same time period.

“Don’t tax you, don’t tax me, tax that fellow behind the tree,” is how a U.S. senator once described ideal tax policy.

In California and elsewhere, the most unpopular taxes are the ones most people see, like the gas tax and property taxes. The only popular taxes are the ones paid by someone else.

So Proposition 40 — the “billionaire tax” — and its first-in-the-country wealth tax should be very popular, since only 200 people would pay it. But the polling has it struggling.

The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.

If the goal is to tax the rich, a wealth tax is a bad way to do it.

Taxes on the wealthy can cause “fire sales” and job losses. Moreover, “temporary” or “one-time” taxes on a few often become permanent taxes on all. And countries like France and Sweden that tried a wealth tax have repealed it.

Beyond that, most Californians think policy shouldn’t aim to tear some people down but instead focus on a rising tide lifting all boats.

Another reason California voters should be wary of Proposition 40 is because it will lose in court. Here are six reasons why, and this list isn’t even exhaustive.

First, the tax is retroactive. It would apply to any billionaire residing in California on January 1, 2026, which is in the past. Sometimes tax effective dates can be retroactive, but not new taxes, and not without fair notice to those who might be affected.

The sponsors could allow the date to be rewritten. But voters don’t know what the effective date will be, which raises a question: what are people actually voting on?

Second, the tax violates the Commerce Clause of the U.S. Constitution. Courts interpret the Constitution to prevent states from taxing more than their fair share of interstate activity. Proposition 40 attempts to tax the assets of California residents, even if these assets are in another state — or another country. Non-resident spouses of California residents can also be taxed. In legal terms, this tax is not fairly apportioned.

Third, Proposition 40 contains a rash of arbitrary rules. The Equal Protection Clause protects everyone from laws that have no rational relation to an important government objective. Proposition 40 has a number of irrational provisions, such as crippling penalties on private valuation experts who estimate assets to be worth less than the state tax authorities do.

Fourth, the tax is an attempt to target specific individuals — what legal experts call a “bill of attainder.” The Constitution prohibits such laws, seeing them as unjust punishment of individuals without a judicial trial.

Fifth, Proposition 40 illegally delegates authority to the legislature. While proponents say the tax is only going to target the wealthiest, and only once, Proposition 40 gives the legislature the power to change the rules as it sees fit, regardless of the property tax limit and voter-approval protections of Proposition 13.

Sixth, courts have long upheld a constitutionally protected right to travel. With its retroactive residency snapshot date, Proposition 40 imposes a punishing tax on former residents after they leave the state, and on new residents who move into the state on or before that date.

All this makes Proposition 40 more than an unusual tax proposal. It is a collection of novel and constitutionally dubious provisions that will provoke litigation from the moment it takes effect.

At the National Taxpayers Union Foundation, we fight for taxpayers in the courtroom. Recently, we won refunds in Colorado for taxpayers who paid an illegally increased property tax. Louisiana restructured its archaic sales tax system after we filed a constitutional challenge in court. We’ve sued the IRS for unfair process and excessive data collection. We know when a state tax has crossed the line.

Maryland learned this lesson the hard way. In 2020, Maryland’s legislature passed a first-in-the-country tax on digital advertising. Because it exempted Maryland businesses while taxing out-of-state businesses, legal experts warned it wouldn’t stand up in court.

Two months ago, judges ruled that Maryland violated due process, the Commerce Clause, and the federal Internet Tax Freedom Act. A separate court held it also violated the First Amendment. Maryland must now refund five years of tax collections, plus interest.

California can avoid all of that legal drama if Proposition 40 fails. But if it passes, don’t lose hope. We at NTUF are ready to see the state in court.

Joseph Bishop-Henchman is Executive Vice President at National Taxpayers Union Foundation.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Rob Kardashian stepped back into the spotlight for a rare public appearance at sister Kim Kardashian’s 46th birthday bash.

The former reality TV star was photographed Tuesday joining his famous family at Baldi, a steakhouse at the Waldorf Astoria Beverly Hills, to mark the occasion.

Rob, 39, kept it casual for the party, sporting a black bomber jacket over a black collared shirt, paired with matching black trousers, black sneakers and a black baseball cap as he hung out outside the restaurant ahead of the festivities.

He was pictured chatting with the birthday girl and sisters Khloé and Kourtney Kardashian, standing out among the trio as they got dolled up for the celebration.

Khloé, 42, wore a sheer nude-pink bodycon dress with matching stilettos, while Kourtney, 47, opted for a dark purple long-sleeved mini dress and black high heels.

Meanwhile, Kim dazzled in a shimmery olive-green mini dress featuring a plunging V-neckline, which she accessorized with a jeweled headpiece.

Later, Rob ditched his jacket and button-down shirt for a simple black Nike T-shirt accessorized with a diamond chain as he exited the shindig alongside Khloé, Kim and mom Kris Jenner.

Kim appeared to have changed into a dark red version of her earlier look, while Kris, 70, opted for a pale yellow floral-embellished coat featuring feathered accents.

Rob, who starred on the first eight seasons of “Keeping Up with the Kardashians” before opting for a more limited role, has largely kept a low profile since 2016.

The family’s original reality show aired for 20 seasons between 2007 and 2021.

He previously addressed his decision to fly under the radar during a July 2025 appearance on Khloé’s podcast, “Khloé in Wonder Land,” revealing, “It just has everything to do with myself.”

“I don’t wanna be filming and putting myself in a position where I’m not comfortable,” Rob told his sister when she asked why he chose not to appear on “The Kardashians” alongside the rest of his family.

“I’m not comfortable in my skin, so why would I want to go be on camera and just be vulnerable and let people in when that’s not what I want to do?” he added.

Still, Rob made a cameo during Season 7 of his family’s Hulu series, which premiered in 2022 and is currently airing its eighth season, with Kim teasing in the trailer that “some familiar faces are back.”

He has also popped up in photos from other family gatherings over the years, most recently appearing in snaps shared by Khloé from her 42nd birthday party in July.

Rob was all smiles as he posed alongside Khloé, Kourtney, Kim and Kris, as well as his 9-year-old daughter, Dream, whom he shares with ex Blac Chyna.

Kim Kardashian linked up with her family for her 46th birthday.

The Skims founder doubled down on chainmail for a Wednesday night dinner at Baldi at the Waldorf Astoria Beverly Hills.

Her new stylist, Law Roach, pulled a pair of coordinating mini caftans from Paco Rabanne’s haute couture fall 1996 couture collection, starting with an emerald green metal mesh and its matching bejeweled headpiece. The dress plunged low in front, and a center slit flashed her black underwear.

She finished the first look with black stiletto mule sandals by Paris Texas ($745).

Once inside, the reality star changed into a blood-red version of the design, accessorized the way it appeared on the runway 30 years ago: with a red beaded headpiece and a matching oversized cross necklace. Both caftans featured batwing sleeves and crystal embellishments.

Mom Kris Jenner, sisters Kylie Jenner, Khloé Kardashian and Kourtney Kardashian, and brother Rob Kardashian all turned out for the occasion.

Video from inside the party shows the birthday girl blowing out the candles on a giant raspberry-covered cake.

Video from inside the party shows the birthday girl blowing out the candles on a giant raspberry-covered cake.

news.originalContent:

A lighter found in the car of the man accused of sparking the deadly Palisades Fire will be “front and center” at his second federal trial — after it was revealed that extensive testing was conducted on the igniter prosecutors say started the blaze.

Jonathan Rinderknecht, who the government has charged with starting the devastating inferno using a green Bic barbecue lighter, appeared in a Los Angeles federal courtroom Thursday ahead of the trial set to begin on Nov. 2.

After the hourlong hearing, Rinderknecht’s attorney Steve Haney revealed details of a video experiment performed on the lighter by the prosecution nine months after his client was arrested.

The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.

Please provide a valid email.

By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

“I don’t know why they didn’t test the lighter before they charged my client, but they did later,” Haney told the California Post.

California Post News: Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, X, YouTube, WhatsApp, LinkedInCalifornia Post Sports Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, XCalifornia Post  Opinion California Post Newsletters: Sign up here!California Post App: Download here!Home delivery: Sign up here!Page Six Hollywood: Sign up here!

The video evidence is believed to show testing of the lighter and the ignition of brush.

“The results of the testing will be front and center on video at the trial,” Haney continued, contending that it will pose a problem for prosecutors.

“The cause of the fire according to the government was a lighter, with no accelerants on a hill on January 1st, and they need to prove that,” he said.

“They didn’t prove it in the first trial, and I think that will be even a bigger challenge based on the new evidence in the second trial.”Haney stressed that the testing was done 11 months after the fire and nine months after his client was arrested.

“It’s going to be a big issue, the second-guessing to test the cause of the fire months after my client was arrested,” he added.

The lighter was discovered by investigators on January 24, 2025, in the glove compartment of Rinderknecht’s car.

During his first trial, which ended in a mistrial after the jury deadlocked, the lighter was shown in the background of a selfie Rinderknecht snapped in his apartment hours before he allegedly sparked the Lachlan Fire on New Year’s.

The Lachlan Fire smoldered for days and re-ignited when record Santa Ana winds hit Pacific Palisades days later, causing a massive inferno, according to prosecutors.

Rinderknecht’s highly publicized first trial ended in a hung jury, with the jurors deadlocked 11-1 in favor of acquittal.

After the first trial, a juror named Bryana from Lompoc told The Post she felt the government didn’t present a convincing enough case.

“It’s disappointing because of how much money and time they put into the same thing. I don’t know … but like, yeah, bullsh–t,” she said.

LA’s top federal prosecutor, Bill Essayli, was quick to declare he would retry Rinderknecht.

“The evidence is strong that Jonathan Rinderknecht is responsible for igniting the fire on January 1, 2025, which eventually became the Palisades fire. We fully intend to retry this case before a new jury and obtain guilty verdicts on all charged counts,” he posted on X at the time.

Rinderknecht is charged with two federal counts of arson and faces a maximum of 45 years behind bars.

Haney is hoping for a full acquittal the second time around.

“There’s some very strong evidence in the second trial that will erode their theory of how that fire even started,” he said.

“I said right from the beginning that he’s no goo
news.originalContent:
What led to LeBron James being labelled a disgrace by US President Donald Trump, who says NBA star disgraced anthem?

President Donald Trump on Thursday accused LeBron James of disrespecting the United States after the NBA star appeared to continue his warm-ups while the national anthem was performed before Philadelphia’s season opener on Tuesday.

“I said right from the beginning that he’s no good, a TOTAL DISGRACE,” Trump said of James in a social media post sharing the video.

“LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!”

James appeared to practise a golf swing and jump shot as The Star-Spangled Banner was performed at Tuesday’s game in New York. James, starting his first season with Philadelphia, was lined up alongside teammates who mostly stood still during the anthem.

Trump and James have been critical of each other for years, occasionally trading public swipes.

James had not made a public comment or a social media post as of Thursday evening about Trump’s gripe.

The 41-year-old James, in his record 24th NBA season, was set to make his home debut for the Sixers Thursday night against Cleveland.

Among some of the more notable times James became entangled with the president or politics:

James was with Cleveland in 2017 when he made a statement during an NBA game with his shoes — one black, one white, with the word “equality” in capital gold letters on the back of each.

Then, after the game, James made a statement about Trump, saying: “This is a beautiful country and we’re never going to let one person dictate how beautiful and how powerful we are.”

James had called Trump  “a bum” on Twitter and also said earlier that season about the president: “He doesn’t understand how many kids, no matter the race, look up to the president of the United States for guidance, for leadership, for words of encouragement. He doesn’t understand that, and that’s what makes me more sick than anything.”

James showed determination to speak out on social issues and the nation’s political climate after Fox News host Laura Ingraham criticised the four-time NBA champion for his 2018 comments about social issues.

“We will definitely not shut up and dribble,” James said. “I will definitely not do that. I mean too much to society. I mean too much to the youth. I mean too much to so many kids that feel like they don’t have a way out and they need someone to help lead them out of the situation they’re in.”

James referenced Muhammad Ali, Jim Brown, Bill Russell and Jackie Robinson as athletes who previously spoke up for equality and change with no concerns about the consequences or any rewards.

“We know it’s bigger than us,” James said.

James was named The Associated Press’s Male Athlete of the Year in 2020 in large part for leading the Los Angeles Lakers to a championship and, at the peak of the Black Lives Matter movement, helping convince many who had never voted to finally head to the polls.

“I still know what I do on the floor and obviously, I give everything to the game,” James said. “But I can make a greater impact off the floor right now, more than I can on the floor. And I want to continue to inspire people with the way I play the game of basketball. But there’s so many more things that I can do off the floor to help cultivate people, inspire people, bring people together, empower them.”

AC Milan striker and former LA Galaxy star Zlatan Ibrahimovic blasted socially conscious athletes in a 2021 interview. Ibrahimovic called it “a mistake” for James and other athletes to get involved in political causes, saying they should “just do what you do best, because it doesn’t look good”.

James, naturally, rejected the criticism.

“I would never shut up about things that are wrong,” James said.

news.originalContent:
A magnitude 7 earthquake hit China’s southwestern region of Tibet at about 10:33pm (14:33 GMT) on Thursday, killing 16 people and injuring 32 others, state ‌news agency Xinhua reported, citing Nagqu City’s emergency management bureau.

Eleven of the injured were in serious condition, while 21 sustained minor injuries, Xinhua added.

A level-II earthquake disaster emergency response was activated in the area, the news agency said.

The US Geological Survey said that the earthquake’s epicentre was in a mountainous area about 190km east-northeast of Nagqu and 390km northeast of the regional capital Lhasa.

Local authorities have found at least two people injured in a village near the epicentre, with some houses in villages closest to the epicentre showing cracks, according to Xinhua.

Videos released by local state media showed people leaving their ⁠homes and seeking shelter outside or in ⁠their cars parked on the street.

The earthquake is ‌the strongest to hit China since January 2024.

news.originalContent:
Judge says Trump must sit for questioning from a BBC lawyer by December 11 or face possible dismissal of lawsuit.

A federal judge in the United States has ordered President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition as part of his $10bn defamation lawsuit against the British broadcaster BBC.

On Thursday, US Magistrate Judge Enjolique Lett ruled that Trump would be required to answer questions under oath in a session with the BBC‘s lawyers.

The deposition is scheduled to take place no later than December 11, or Trump could face sanctions, including the possible dismissal of the lawsuit.

Trump had previously been scheduled to sit for deposition on October 16 but had cancelled due to a “matter of national importance”.

Charles Tobin, a lawyer for the BBC, said that the president was in fact campaigning in the state of Georgia on that day.

“He was participating in party politics and prioritised that over sitting for the deposition,” Tobin said.

The BBC lawsuit is one of several he has launched against news outlets over coverage he dislikes or casts as unfair.

Trump is currently enmeshed in another $10bn defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal that he refiled in May after it was previously dismissed. Another defamation case seeks $15bn in damages from The New York Times and Penguin Random House, a book publisher.

That streak of litigation has alarmed press freedom advocates who say that the president frequently uses government pressure and legal threats to shape coverage in his favour.

His case against the BBC centres on a documentary it aired, titled Trump: A Second Chance.

The documentary features clips of a speech Trump made on January 6, 2021, the day that Trump supporters later attacked the US Capitol.

Trump has said that a clip from his speech was misleadingly edited to suggest he encouraged attendees to storm the Capitol, the seat of the US Congress. Legislators inside had been in the process of certifying Trump’s 2020 election defeat at the time of the riot.

The British broadcaster has acknowledged that filmmakers spliced together different segments of Trump’s remarks on January 6.

The head of the BBC and its top news executive both resigned, and the outlet issued an apology. But the network has denied Trump’s defamation claims.

Trump has maintained that he never told his supporters to commit violence in a bid to prevent the peaceful transition of power.

Trump, however, has long pushed the false claim that his loss in the 2020 race was due to election-rigging.

On January 6, 2021, Trump had gathered his supporters on the Ellipse outside the White House to reiterate his unsubstantiated assertions.

During his speech, he encouraged them to “fight like hell” and refused to concede to what he falsely portrayed as an election stolen through “fraud”.

Trump and his allies oversaw a multifaceted effort to stay in power despite his loss, one that included the alleged recruitment of “false electors” to cast fraudulent Electoral College votes on his behalf.

He later faced federal charges of attempting to overturn the 2020 election, which were dropped upon his re-election in 2024.

Separately, a state-level case in Georgia accused Trump of engaging in a criminal conspiracy to subvert the 2020 election. The case was dismissed in November 2025 after a replacement prosecutor took over following the disqualification of Fani Willis, who brought the charges against Trump.

A congressional probe into the events around January 6 concluded that the president had been reluctant to call on his supporters to stand down after they stormed the Capitol.

Trump and his allies oversaw a multifaceted effort to stay in power despite his loss, one that included the alleged recruitment of “false electors” to cast fraudulent Electoral College votes on his behalf.

He later faced federal charges of attempting to overturn the 2020 election, which were dropped upon his re-election in 2024.

Separately, a state-level case in Georgia accused Trump of engaging in a criminal conspiracy to subvert the 2020 election. The case was dismissed in November 2025 after a replacement prosecutor took over following the disqualification of Fani Willis, who brought the charges against Trump.

A congressional probe into the events around January 6 concluded that the president had been reluctant to call on his supporters to stand down after they stormed the Capitol.

news.originalContent:
Photo by Jemal Countess/Getty Images for Accountable Tech

A state attorney general’s legal victory resulted in Meta having to pay a historic-level fine — which may have dire consequences for free expression online, experts say.

New Mexico District Court Judge Francis J. Mathew on Wednesday ordered Meta to pay a $25 billion fine after a jury found that the company had misled consumers about its privacy policies. Democratic New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez sued Meta’s platform Facebook, claiming that the company mishandled New Mexicans’ personal information.

Free speech advocates warn that this may stifle free speech by threatening fines against those who do not sufficiently crack down on alleged hate speech and misinformation.

“This decision is a major threat to free speech. It would allow a few lawyers in a few states to regulate speech online in violation of federal law and the First Amendment. I hope Meta sticks to its guns and appeals this decision to protect not only its own rights, but everyone’s,” Casey Mattox, a constitutional attorney and vice president of legal strategy for Stand Together, told the Daily Caller News Foundation.

“This is a historic day for New Mexico and for consumers across the country. For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law. A New Mexico jury found nearly 44 million violations of our consumer protection statute, and this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences,” Attorney General Torrez said in a statement on Wednesday, according to the New Mexico Department of Justice. “We took on one of the largest companies in the world because New Mexicans deserve honesty, accountability, and the protection of their personal information. Today’s result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable.”

Torrez’s office did not immediately respond to a DCNF comment request.

The fine against Meta far exceeds what many national governments have levied against alleged fraudsters and others in alleged antitrust violations.

The $25 billion fine against Meta is more than double the state’s annual budget, per its fiscal year 2027 budget overview and exceeds the largest fine ever issued by the Department of Justice when then-Attorney General Eric Holder issued a $16 billion fine against Bank of America in 2014 for financial fraud leading up to the 2008 financial crisis, per an archived Justice Department press release. Meta’s fine is more than five times the largest fine issued by the European Union, when the supranational government issued a €4.1 billion antitrust fine against Google in July, per Reuters. (RELATED: After Amazon Slammed The Door, Meta Rallies Partners To Welcome AI Shoppers)

Meta plans to appeal the decision, saying that the attorney general seeks to enforce free speech policies.

“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico. At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online,” C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s Chief Legal Officer, said in a statement to the DCNF.

“We are confident we will prevail on appeal,” added Mahoney, who previously served as Deputy United States Trade Representative during the first Trump administration. “In the meantime, Meta will continue to build a safe and free platform to connect millions of Americans, grow small businesses, and help the country maintain its competitive edge.”

Torrez’s political career benefitted from significant donations from leftist megadonor George Soros.

When he successfully ran for Bernalillo County district attorney, the leftist super PAC New Mexico Safety & Justice, which was funded by Soros, spent roughly $93,000 in media buys backing Torrez plus an additional $11,500 in polling, the New Mexico Political Report noted in 2016.

Simon Kubiak, Torrez’s Republican opponent at the time, soon dropped out of the race.

“New Mexicans cannot afford to challenge anyone who has unlimited resources and support from a multibillionaire from another country,” Kubiak said in 2016, in an apparent reference to Soros, according to the New Mexico Political Report.

A substantial part of the violations laid against Meta involved statements about Meta’s alleged inability to curb alleged “hate speech” and “misinformation.”

The judgment for the case found “Facebook promises regarding the prevalence and nature of misinformation and hate speech on the platform and assured the public that the users on the platform would, no matter who they were, be treated equally. The jury found those statements to be false as well,” according to the court’s conclusions of law.

“Facebook made repeated statements to the public respecting its ability to identify and remove hate speech and misinformation despite knowing those statements to be deceptive,” the court’s findings of facts stated.

The findings of fact stated that Facebook’s internal system, including its “CrossCheck” or “XCheck,” often allowed content that purportedly violated the platform’s misinformation policy to stay up and accrue millions of views.

“In its many statements respecting hate speech and misinformation, Facebook disclosed the extent or impact of the XCheck system,” the court stated in its findings.

“New Mexico found a way to fine platforms for speech it didn’t delete,” Ken Macon of Reclaim The Net, wrote in early October about the suit against Meta.

During the openings and closings, lawyers for New Mexico accused Meta of dropping its third-party fact-checking to gain favor with President Donald Trump.

The lawyers told the jury that when Trump “came into office for the second time in January of last year, January 2025, and he was one of the people who didn’t like having information removed or flagged, [Meta CEO Mark] Zuckerberg announced they were canceling the third-party fact checkers and firing all of them,” according to a source who shared their knowledge of the trial.

The state argued that “because nobody likes being fact-checked, particularly people in power, when Trump ascends to the presidency again … Facebook announces we’re getting rid of third-party, fact-checking program,” the source added. The lawyers for New Mexico said that was “just a coincidence.”

During the court case, the jury was shown internal Meta emails about Joe Rogan, the popular podcaster whose show Zuckerberg had appeared on. Zuckerberg in September 2023 sent an email asking that Rogan’s account be put on a “list of accounts that we double review before taking action on them” to reduce false flags of policy violations that may lead to a deleted account,” the source continued.

Other critics warned that the fine against Meta serves as a pressure campaign to stifle free speech on its platforms.

“New Mexico’s Attorney General should not dictate what Americans can say online or use massive financial penalties to pressure companies into censorship. Meta has stood for free speech, and we hope the higher courts will uphold the First Amendment and put an end to this abuse of power,” Jordan Sekulow, the president of the American Center for Law and Justice, wrote on X this week.

New Mexico’s Attorney General should not dictate what Americans can say online or use massive financial penalties to pressure companies into censorship. Meta has stood for free speech, and we hope the higher courts will uphold the First Amendment and put an end to this abuse of power.

“New Mexico’s Attorney General shouldn’t get to use a $25 billion penalty to strong-arm Meta into censoring speech. Meta already ditched the biased third-party fact-checkers who could kill a post’s reach with a label. Higher courts need to stop this clear attempt to punish free expression,” Christian Collins, the founder and president of the Texas Youth Summit, wrote on X this week.

In January 2025, Meta announced it would end its fact-checking program move to a community notes model to allow more speech.

“Some people believe giving more people a voice is driving division rather than bringing us together. More people across the spectrum believe that achieving the political outcomes they think matter is more important than every person having a voice. I think that’s dangerous,” Zuckerberg said during a 2019 speech at Georgetown University about how limiting free speech may reinforce institutions rather than empowering people, according to a Meta press release. (RELATED: Facebook Announces Official End Date For Fact-Checking Program)

The New Mexico attorney general said Facebook once “bragged” about the company’s prior fact-check regime but “when Donald Trump wins the presidency again a second time …Facebook announces we’re getting rid of their fact-check program, and we’re just going to what everybody else has — the community notes program,” according to the Daily Wire.

The New Mexico Democratic attorney general said he and other Democratic attorneys general have met “daily” for the first 90 days to strategize lawsuits, Fox News reported in January.

news.originalContent:
(Photo by KENZO TRIBOUILLARD/AFP via Getty Images)

European regulators are relying on bureaucratic intimidation against U.S. tech platforms to censor Americans on American soil, attorneys battling these foreign attempts to regulate online free speech told the Daily Caller.

These regulations present themselves as the United Kingdom’s Online Safety Act of 2023 (OSA) and the European Union’s Digital Services Act (DSA), both of which have attempted to levy heavy fines from across the pond on American digital platforms with the goal of limiting American free speech, a lawyer involved in each case told the Caller. (RELATED: Americans Who Moved To Europe Share Their Immediate Regret, Horror)

Preston Byrne, a dual-qualified attorney in the U.K. and U.S. who currently represents “every known company to have publicly refused one of [the Office of Communications’ (Ofcom)] orders,” told the Caller that the U.K. may have just won a legal battle in U.S. courts, but it has lost the war.

After accusing American platforms like 4chan of failing to comply with mandatory administrative safety duties, Ofcom demanded internal operational data from these U.S. businesses, threatening fines of up to 10 percent of their annual global turnover.

“Fuck you,” Byrne said, describing his initial sentiment towards the threats to the Caller. “We’re not going to obey your illegal and unconstitutional orders. And so we sued them.”

We’ve fined 4chan £450,000 for not having age checks in place to prevent children seeing porn on its site. The Online Safety Act is concerned with protecting people in the UK. It doesn’t require platforms to restrict what people in other countries see. 🔗https://t.co/m2QUapVHjv https://t.co/9rba57bHiq

While the U.S. federal court dismissed the lawsuit on foreign sovereign immunity grounds, the judge noted that American courts generally decline to enforce foreign judgments that violate the Constitution and may not be required to enforce foreign penal judgments.

“If you want to tell Americans what we can and can’t do on U.S. soil,” Byrne said, “you’re going to have to send battleships.”

Yet official notices from Ofcom persist, with threats of fines and jail time often sent directly to small American website owners’ addresses. While unenforceable, Byrne said these notices still censor American free speech, as American targets “immediately roll over and comply,” which he says changes the information environment within the U.S.

Byrne said they have even asked Ofcom to block the websites in the U.K. altogether rather than continuing to tell Americans how to operate their businesses.

“If you’re going to block a website in the United Kingdom because it’s non-compliant with your law, that is a British sovereign decision that they can make for themselves,” Byrne said. “But what they’re doing now is saying, ‘if you don’t obey us, we will fine you, we will jail you.’”

The UK might claim that services wholly operated in the US fall under UK law, but unless you’re prepared to send an invasion fleet across the Atlantic, they do not fall under UK law. UK law could claim the Moon is made of cheese. Wouldn’t make it true. https://t.co/4LdoH5LHLw

The only long-term solution, Byrne said, would be American legislation that could ensure such notices are not even delivered to the U.S., as they would be seen as an attempt to intimidate or threaten Americans from exercising their constitutional right to free speech.

The legislation, he said, should let Americans sue Ofcom, where officials would fear losing in an American court and stop sending the notices altogether.

For those reasons, Byrne cited the HOMEFRONT Act and the GRANITE Act as key legislative and nonpartisan mechanisms to protect American citizens and tech platforms.

While Byrne is pushing for swift legislative action to stop foreign threat notices at the water’s edge, Jeremy Tedesco, senior counsel and senior vice president at Alliance Defending Freedom, warned that timing is critical. Without a congressional shield explicitly barring foreign censorship, Tedesco told the Caller, a future White House less committed to the First Amendment could actively help European regulators enforce speech restrictions against American platforms that run afoul of the administration’s political agenda.

“We think ultimately that the best solution to this problem is a law from Congress stopping the foreign governments, whether it’s the E.U. or the U.K. or anyone else, from enforcing their content bans and their fines on American companies,” Tedesco told the Caller while pointing to the Biden administration’s attempt to censor free speech online.

Foreign censors have no right to threaten Americans with fines or arrest for protected speech hosted on American soil. Yet regulators like Ofcom can’t be held accountable for these gross violations of free expression because they hide behind the veil of sovereign immunity. The GRANITE Act strips away that immunity so Americans can finally haul these foreign censors into U.S. court and teach them what the First Amendment means.

Tedesco, who is challenging the E.U.’s DSA, an equivalent of the OSA, in European courts, told the Caller that the E.U.’s version of the law is “incredibly vague” and “allows the DSA enforcement officials to ultimately come up with whatever reason they want to punish speech they don’t like.”

In its first noncompliance decision under the DSA, the European Commission fined Elon Musk’s U.S.-based social media platform X €120 million, citing alleged transparency violations.

Tedesco warned the EU’s demand for internal data under the DSA is a calculated move to set up future enforcement against Musk. By requiring X to hand over data to European-funded “researchers,” the E.U. could essentially embed external auditors in the company, and fine it for failing to suppress what they deem hate speech or misinformation.

We’ve accepted X’s action plan to meet its DSA obligations on transparency and researchers’ access to data. These approved measures are an important step in enabling researchers, civil society and the public to gain more transparency into X’s systems. 🔗https://t.co/fRfJN9kTXb https://t.co/ZM7NvXwz2Z

“So I think it was a really smart idea by the European Commission to go after things that don’t look like they really affect speech, but they do,” Tedesco said.

He said Americans need to fight the urge to not care what Europeans are doing, since Europeans care a lot about what U.S. citizens say online. (RELATED: Europe’s Riots Take Terrifying Turn As Anti-Terror Police Investigate Arson, Reports Of Armed Rioters Surface)

“I just think Americans need to wake up to the fact that their speech online isn’t free until foreign regulations like the DSA and the OSA are revoked,” Tedesco implored while also referring to similar laws in Australia and Russia. “The fight over there is really a fight on American soil for free speech.”

news.originalContent:
The Irish government released an advertisement Tuesday depicting grandparents hugging their grandchildren in an effort to combat rape.

Ireland’s taxpayer-funded Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) faced criticism from Irish lawmakers for a TV advertisement promoting consent. The DRCC released an advertisement for the We-Consent campaign showing grandparents hugging their granddaughter – without the granddaughter’s approval.

The latest ad from the Irish Government to the Irish people, who are the font of all problems in the country and desperately need to be stopped from their bad behaviour. This time, it’s hugging your grandkids. https://t.co/IKYKteKP8m

“Not everyone wants a hug, even from the people who love them,” the DRCC advertisement says. Facing backlash, the advertisement was quickly scrubbed on Tuesday, the BBC reported. The DRCC did not immediately reply to the Daily Caller News Foundation’s request for comment.

“[The advertisement] was both inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents,” Irish Fianna Fáil politician Jim O’Callaghan told the BBC.

“Embarrassed for all the people that think that this is a literal rather than a figurative message…and have forgotten that advertising creativity is a thing,” Ireland’s Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Councillor Lorraine Hall said on X, defending the advertisement. (RELATED: MOREFIELD: The New Kind Of Woke Is Worse Than The Old)

The DRCC created the advertisement using feedback compiled from over 20 consent workshops discussing scenarios that made participants feel uncomfortable, The Irish Times reported.

The Irish government’s CUAN is a statutory agency established in 2024 to provide resources to organizations assisting victims of sexual assault, including the DRCC. CUAN’s budget increased from €54 million to €79 million in 2026, according to the CUAN 2025 annual report.

“The mission of Dublin Rape Crisis Centre is to prevent the harm and heal the trauma of rape and other forms of sexual violence,” the mission statement of the We-Consent campaign states.

The DRCC’s advertisement comes in the wake of European efforts to address an uptick in sexual violence. “Between 2014 and 2024, sexual violence offences jumped by 94% (+124 350 cases) and rape offences by 150% (+58 983),” the European Union reported. Ireland reported a 43% higher rate of sexual violence than its EU counterparts in 2023, according to The Law Society of Ireland.

(Photo by John Tully/Getty Images)

Republicans might have accidentally given Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom and the California legislature the keys that will end up shaping some of the most important rules involving artificial intelligence.

Politico reported Wednesday that Anthropic’s draft federal AI safety bill, which the company is pitching to lawmakers on Capitol Hill, was directly influenced by California law. The bill lays out the potential risk thresholds at which the government would be allowed to intervene and block an AI model. But unfortunately for Republicans, Newsom and the California legislature had the free opportunity to lay the groundwork and define the arbitrary risk thresholds that could end up triggering federal intervention. (RELATED: Anthropic Floats Bill That Would Let Feds Step In Only When More Than 50 Lives Are On The Line)
